_meta: A worker being shut down while it has requests in flight and new requests still arriving, used to show why shutdown must DRAIN -- stop accepting new work, then let the in-flight requests finish before terminating -- rather than hard-kill, which drops everything in progress. A worker in a fleet is stopped constantly: a deploy rolls it, an autoscaler scales it in, an operator restarts it. At the instant of shutdown the worker is usually busy: it holds requests that are partway done. A hard stop terminates the process immediately, so every in-flight request is abandoned mid-work -- the client sees an error or a timeout for work that was almost complete, and any partial side effects are left dangling. A graceful drain instead does two things in order: first it stops accepting NEW requests (so incoming work is rejected at the door and routed to a healthy worker instead of being taken on and then dropped), and then it processes the in-flight requests through to completion before the process exits. The result is that no in-flight request is lost -- it either completes here or, if it had not started, was rejected up front so the caller could retry elsewhere. inflight is the set of requests already in progress when the shutdown signal arrives, each with an id; new_arrivals is the set of requests that arrive during the shutdown window. These are the fixture; under a hard stop vs a graceful drain, the completed set, the lost set (accepted work that was abandoned), and the rejected set (new work turned away for a healthy worker) are computed.
